subject: Islamic Studies
board: TGA Islamic Studies scheme (aqeedah, fiqh, seerah, hadith, akhlaq)
source: Drive: RE folder and Islamic Studies schemes folder checked (Edexcel Int. GCSE Islamic Studies spec and KS4 SOW only; no KS2 material) - adapted to the TGA Islamic Studies scheme from own knowledge, with Qur'an/hadith only from well-known authentic sources

lessons.title: Who is Allah? Tawhid, the Oneness of Allah
objectives: Explain that Tawhid means Allah is One
Recite and explain the meaning of Surah al-Ikhlas
Give examples of things that only Allah can do

keywords.def: believing that Allah is One, with no partner
Lord: the One who creates, owns, cares for and controls everything
the Eternal Refuge whom all creation needs while He needs none
worship: everything we do to please Allah alone

starter: Say the bismillah aloud. What does it mean in English?
Name three things Allah has created that you can see from your window.
What is the first pillar of Islam, and what words do we say for it?

teach.heading: Bismillah: starting with Allah
bullets: We begin in the name of Allah, the Most Kind, the Most Merciful
Allah is our Creator, our Lord (Rabb)
Today: what does it mean that Allah is One?
teach.note: Begin with bismillah together. Ask: why do Muslims start things with Allah’s name? Take 2-3 answers (to get blessing, to remember Him, to do good). Link to the kalimah they already know. Misconception to listen for: that Allah is ‘like’ something we can picture. Say gently that we do not imagine Allah’s form.

teach.heading: What does Tawhid mean?
bullets: Tawhid means believing Allah is One
He has no partner, no helper and no children
Only Allah creates, owns and controls everything
Only Allah deserves to be worshipped
teach.note: Write ‘ahad’ = one, unique. Give the example of a school: there is one headteacher in charge, but nobody is in charge of Allah. Careful: analogies are only for understanding, nothing is like Allah (Qur’an 42:11, say it in simple English: ‘There is nothing like Him’). Ask: what could someone worship wrongly (idols, money, fame)?

teach.heading: Surah al-Ikhlas (112)
bullets: “Say: He is Allah, the One.”
“Allah, the Eternal Refuge.”
“He neither begets nor is born.”
“And there is none equal to Him.”
teach.note: Recite the surah slowly in Arabic then read the meaning. Explain ‘as-Samad’: everyone needs Him, He needs no one. Ask: who do you need every day? (parents, food, water) Then: does Allah need any of these? Highlight: this short surah sums up Tawhid. Many reports tell us it is a great surah; just say we love to recite it in our prayers.

teach.heading: Only Allah
bullets: Allah gives life and takes it back
Allah provides rizq: food, water, health
Allah hears every du’a, near or far
So we ask Allah alone for help
teach.note: Link to Surah al-Fatihah: ‘You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help.’ Ask: when you are scared or ill, who do you call upon? Give the idea that we can ask people for help they are able to give (a teacher helps with homework) but we ask Allah for what only He can do (to guide hearts, to heal, to forgive).

teach.heading: Living with Tawhid
bullets: Pray to Allah only
Put trust in Allah after working hard
Be grateful: say alhamdulillah
Be honest, because Allah sees us
teach.note: Make it practical. ‘Tawakkul’ means trust: explain it as ‘do your best, then rely on Allah’. Take 2 volunteers to give a real-life example (before a test, when losing something).

practice: Complete the sentence: Tawhid means believing that ______.
Match the ayah to its meaning: ‘Allahus-Samad’ / ‘Lam yalid wa lam yulad’ / ‘Qul huwa Allahu ahad’.
Give two things that only Allah can do and two things people can do.
independent: Write four sentences explaining Tawhid to a younger child in Year 2.
Draw and label a poster for Surah al-Ikhlas with each ayah and its meaning.
List three ways we show we believe in Tawhid at home or school.
exit: What does Tawhid mean?
Why is Allah called as-Samad?
lessons.homework: Learn Surah al-Ikhlas by heart with its meaning and write one sentence about each ayah.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the surah with transliteration and a picture clue for each ayah; stretch: explain why Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.

lessons.title: The Beautiful Names of Allah
objectives: Know that Allah has beautiful names
Explain the meaning of at least six names
Say how a Muslim can reflect on these names in daily life

keywords.def: the most beautiful names of Allah
the Most Gracious, whose mercy covers everything
the Most Merciful, especially to the believers
the Creator

starter: What does Tawhid mean?
Recite Surah al-Ikhlas together and give its meaning.
Name one thing only Allah can do.

teach.heading: Allah has beautiful names
bullets: “To Allah belong the best names, so call upon Him by them” (7:180)
Each name tells us about Allah’s perfect qualities
We learn them from the Qur’an and authentic Sunnah
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Explain that we know Allah’s names only from what He and His Messenger ﷺ told us; we do not make up names. Ask: why do we learn names of people we love? Link to getting to know Allah better. Sound idea: we call on Allah by names that fit our du’a, for example ‘Ya Ghafur, forgive me’.

teach.heading: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim
bullets: Ar-Rahman: Allah’s mercy reaches all creation
Ar-Rahim: His special mercy for believers
Both are in the bismillah and al-Fatihah
teach.note: Show the bismillah and point at the two names. Ask: what are signs of mercy you can see in the world (rain, sunlight, a mother’s love)? Point out that all mercy in the world comes from Allah. Misconception: that Allah’s mercy means there is no accountability. Say we hope for His mercy and still try our best.

teach.heading: Al-Khaliq, Ar-Razzaq, as-Sami’
bullets: Al-Khaliq: the Creator who made everything
Ar-Razzaq: the Provider of all provision
As-Sami’: the All-Hearing
Al-Basir: the All-Seeing
teach.note: Use real examples: how does a seed grow into fruit? Who provides? Then: Allah hears a whisper from under the blanket at night. Ask: how should knowing Allah sees us change our behaviour when no one is looking? Link to honesty in tests.

teach.heading: Al-Ghafur and At-Tawwab
bullets: Al-Ghafur: the Forgiving
At-Tawwab: the One who accepts repentance
We say astaghfirullah when we make mistakes
We forgive others too
teach.note: Explain tawbah simply: stop the wrong, feel sorry, promise not to return, and put it right with anyone harmed. Ask: when someone says sorry to you what should you do? Keep a calm, hopeful tone: Allah loves those who return to Him (Qur’an 2:222 says Allah loves those who repent; you may mention this in your own words).

teach.heading: Using the names in our lives
bullets: Remember Allah in good times and hard times
Call on Allah with a fitting name in du’a
Try to show mercy, honesty and kindness
teach.note: Model a du’a: ‘Ya Razzaq, provide for me what is good.’ Ask pupils to choose a name that suits a situation (feeling worried, wanting to be forgiven). Remind them that we reflect good character, we are never like Allah, but He loves mercy in people.

practice: Match each name with its meaning: Al-Khaliq, Ar-Razzaq, As-Sami’, Al-Ghafur.
Which name would you use in a du’a when you have made a mistake? Explain why.
Fill in the missing word: Ar-Rahman means the Most ______.
independent: Make a colourful mind map with six names of Allah, their meanings and one example of each in daily life.
Write a short du’a using at least two names of Allah.
Explain in three sentences why it helps a Muslim to know Allah’s names.
exit: Give the meaning of two names of Allah.
Why should we only use names of Allah that come from the Qur’an and Sunnah?
lessons.homework: Learn six names of Allah with their meanings and use one in a du’a this evening.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: name cards with picture clues and Arabic/English pairs; stretch: explain the difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim.

lessons.title: Signs of Allah in creation
objectives: Explain what an ayah (sign) of Allah is
Give examples of signs in the universe
Respond to creation with gratitude and care

keywords.def: a sign; also a verse of the Qur’an
everything Allah has made
gratitude to Allah
a trustee who looks after the earth

starter: Give the meaning of Ar-Razzaq and Al-Khaliq.
Say two names of Allah that show mercy.
What does ‘Subhanallah’ mean when we say it?

teach.heading: Signs for people who think
bullets: “In the creation of the heavens and the earth ... are signs for people of understanding” (3:190)
Allah invites us to look, think and wonder
Science and faith both begin with noticing
teach.note: Start with bismillah. Read Qur’an 3:190 in English slowly. Ask pupils what they notice in nature on the way to school or from their window. Point out that Islam encourages reflection. Avoid presenting faith and science as enemies; observing the world is a way to see Allah’s signs.

teach.heading: Signs in the sky and the earth
bullets: The sun gives light and warmth at the right distance
Night and day follow one another
Rain brings dead land back to life
Mountains, seas and animals show Allah’s wisdom
teach.note: Bring in age-appropriate facts: the water cycle, the rotation of the earth for day and night. Ask: what would happen if the sun were much closer? Draw out the idea of balance and order. Remember: we say the universe points to a Creator, we are not pretending to prove everything in 45 minutes.

teach.heading: Signs in ourselves
bullets: Our eyes, hearts and brains work together
Every person is different, with a different voice
Allah gave us the ability to think and speak
teach.note: Link to Qur’an 51:21 (‘and in yourselves, will you not see?’) as a pointer in your own words. Ask: which part of the body amazes you most? Let pupils share. Pause for a moment of silent reflection or a collective ‘Subhanallah’.

teach.heading: How do we respond?
bullets: Say Subhanallah and Alhamdulillah
Thank Allah for His blessings
Look after the earth: do not waste water or food
Be kind to animals and plants
teach.note: Explain that humans are trustees (khalifah) on the earth, so littering and wasting are not good character. Ask for one practical action at home. You may mention that the Prophet ﷺ was kind to animals, to keep the point warm, without quoting a specific wording.

practice: Write two signs of Allah from the sky and two from the earth.
Complete: When I see a beautiful sunset I can say ______.
Explain in a sentence why looking after the environment is part of being grateful.
independent: Draw a ‘Signs of Allah’ poster with six examples and a caption for each.
Write a paragraph beginning ‘I see the signs of Allah when ...’.
Make a pledge card with three actions that care for the earth.
exit: What is an ayah in the sense of a sign?
Give one way a Muslim can show thanks for creation.
lessons.homework: Go for a short walk or look out of a window and list five signs of Allah you notice, with a dhikr phrase for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use photographs for discussion and sentence starters; stretch: explain how reflecting on creation can strengthen iman.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The Six Pillars of Iman
lessons.title: What is Iman? The hadith of Jibril
objectives: Explain what iman means
Name the six pillars of iman in order
Describe the setting of the hadith of Jibril

keywords.def: faith: believing in the heart and showing it by words and actions
a main foundation or support
the angel who brought revelation to the Prophets
Allah’s decree: everything happens by His knowledge and will

starter: Name one sign of Allah in creation.
What does ayah mean?
Why do Muslims say alhamdulillah?

teach.heading: A visitor in white
bullets: Umar ibn al-Khattab told this hadith, recorded by Muslim
A man in white clothes, with no sign of travel, came to the Prophet ﷺ
He asked about Islam, iman and ihsan
He was the angel Jibril, teaching the Companions their religion
teach.note: Tell it as a story. The Prophet ﷺ finished by telling Umar that this was Jibril who came to teach them their religion. Ask: why would the angel come to ask questions instead of just telling? (so that the Companions could hear the answers). This is reported by Imam Muslim; also in other collections.

teach.heading: The six pillars of iman
bullets: Belief in Allah
Belief in His angels
Belief in His books
Belief in His messengers
Belief in the Last Day
Belief in al-Qadr, the good and bad of it
teach.note: In the hadith the Prophet ﷺ said iman is to believe in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and to believe in the divine decree, its good and its bad. Teach a hand-and-heart gesture for each. Misconception: ‘five pillars’ vs ‘six pillars’. Five pillars are what we do; six pillars of iman are what we believe.

teach.heading: Iman and Islam
bullets: Islam: the five actions such as salah and fasting
Iman: what we believe in the heart
Ihsan: worship as if you see Allah
If you do not see Him, He sees you
teach.note: Present a simple table. For ihsan, read the meaning slowly: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, know that He sees you. Ask: how can ihsan make your prayer better? (Focus, slowing down.)

teach.heading: Strengthening our iman
bullets: Learn about Allah and His book
Make dhikr and du’a
Do good deeds and keep good company
Ask Allah to keep our hearts firm
teach.note: Iman increases with obedience and can weaken with sins; ahl as-sunnah hold this view. At Year 6 level, say it as ‘like a plant that needs water’. Ask pupils to pick one practical step.

practice: List the six pillars of iman in order.
True or false: Jibril came as a stranger to teach the Companions. Explain.
What is the difference between Islam and iman?
independent: Draw six pillars and label each with a one-line explanation.
Write four sentences retelling the hadith of Jibril in your own words.
Make a ‘ways to increase iman’ checklist with five ideas.
exit: Name the six pillars of iman.
What does ihsan mean?
lessons.homework: Teach the six pillars of iman to someone at home and write down their response.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pillars on picture cards to sequence; stretch: explain why belief and action go together.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The Six Pillars of Iman
lessons.title: Belief in the angels and the holy books
objectives: Describe the angels and name four of them with their tasks
Name the revealed books
Explain why Muslims believe the Qur’an is preserved

keywords.def: honoured servants of Allah created from light who always obey Him
the book revealed to Prophet Musa (peace be upon him)
the book revealed to Prophet Isa (peace be upon him)
the final word of Allah revealed to Prophet Muhammad ﷺ

starter: List the six pillars of iman.
What is ihsan?
Who asked the Prophet ﷺ the questions in the hadith of Jibril?

teach.heading: Who are the angels?
bullets: Angels are created from light
They obey Allah and never disobey
We cannot normally see them
Belief in them is the second pillar
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. The hadith of Aisha in Sahih Muslim says angels were created from light, jinn from smokeless fire and Adam from what was described to you. Ask pupils: why believe in what we cannot see? (We trust Allah’s word, as we trust air exists though invisible.) Misconception: angels are not female or children of Allah and are not worshipped.

teach.heading: Four angels and their tasks
bullets: Jibril: brings revelation to the prophets
Mikail: in charge of rain and provision
Israfil: will blow the trumpet on the Last Day
The angel of death takes souls by Allah’s command
teach.note: Qur’an 32:11 speaks of ‘the angel of death who has been entrusted with you’; use that description rather than a personal name, since the Qur’an and authentic Sunnah do not name him. Also mention the recording angels (Qur’an 82:10-12). Ask: how does knowing angels record deeds change how we act?

teach.heading: The revealed books
bullets: Suhuf of Ibrahim (scrolls)
Tawrah to Musa and Zabur to Dawud
Injil to Isa
Qur’an to Muhammad ﷺ
teach.note: All the messengers brought the same core message: worship Allah alone. Muslims respect the earlier books as revealed, but the earlier texts were not preserved in their original form. The Qur’an is the final revelation and Allah promised to protect it (15:9: ‘Indeed it is We who sent down the Reminder and indeed We will guard it’).

teach.heading: The Qur’an is preserved
bullets: Memorised by the Companions and written down
Collected into one book under Abu Bakr and copied under Uthman
Millions of huffaz keep it in memory
Same Arabic text across the world
teach.note: Keep the facts simple and accurate: the revelation was written on materials and memorised; Abu Bakr gathered the pages into one collection after the battle of Yamamah on Umar’s advice; Uthman made copies from it. Ask: how do huffaz protect the Qur’an today?

teach.heading: Our response
bullets: Recite the Qur’an daily
Understand and follow its teachings
Respect the Qur’an: keep it clean and high
Love the angels and the messengers
teach.note: Invite one or two pupils to share what they are reciting at present. Stress that the response to belief is action: learn, read, apply.

practice: Match: Jibril / Mikail / Israfil to their task.
List the four books named in the lesson and the prophet each came to.
Why do Muslims believe the Qur’an is protected?
independent: Make a fact file on one angel using only what we know from the Qur’an and Sunnah.
Create a timeline of the revealed books.
Write a short paragraph: ‘What difference does belief in angels make to my day?’
exit: What are angels created from?
Name two holy books and their prophets.
lessons.homework: Recite your current surah to a family member and write one thing you learned from its meaning.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a matching grid with images; stretch: explain similarities and differences between earlier books and the Qur’an.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: The Six Pillars of Iman
lessons.title: Messengers, the Last Day and al-Qadr
objectives: Explain why Allah sent messengers
Describe what Muslims believe about the Last Day
Give a simple explanation of al-Qadr

keywords.def: prophet: a man chosen by Allah to receive revelation
messenger: a prophet given a new message and law
the life after death
relying on Allah after taking the means

starter: Name two angels and their tasks.
Which book was revealed to Prophet Dawud?
Which pillar of iman comes fifth?

teach.heading: Why did Allah send messengers?
bullets: To teach us to worship Allah alone
To show us how to live well
To bring good news and warnings
All messengers brought the same core message
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Name some: Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ (peace be upon them all). Ask pupils what they know about one. Note that we say ‘peace be upon him’ for each prophet. Qur’an 16:36 says Allah sent a messenger to every nation to worship Allah and avoid false gods.

teach.heading: The final messenger
bullets: Muhammad ﷺ is the last prophet
“The Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets” (33:40)
His message is for all people
We love him by following his sunnah
teach.note: Ask: what does ‘Seal’ mean (the last)? Give the stamp analogy. Contrast gently: we love the Prophet ﷺ by obeying him, not by adding to the religion. Connect to the next three lessons on his life.

teach.heading: The Last Day
bullets: Everyone will be raised and questioned
Good deeds will be weighed
Jannah is for those who believe and do good
We hope for Allah’s mercy and fear His justice
teach.note: Keep calm and hopeful. Qur’an 99:7-8: whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it. Ask: why does justice matter? Avoid frightening detail; stress accountability and mercy.

teach.heading: Al-Qadr: Allah’s decree
bullets: Allah knows everything before it happens
Nothing happens outside His knowledge
We still choose and are responsible for our actions
Hardships can be a test and a mercy
teach.note: Give a simple example: a teacher may know which pupils will revise, but knowing does not force them to. Be careful not to over-explain; a Year 6 pupil needs the sense that Allah’s knowledge is perfect and that we must still make an effort. Link to ‘do your best and rely on Allah’ and to sabr.

teach.heading: Putting the pillars together
bullets: Beliefs shape our actions
Hope and responsibility go together
Ask Allah for firmness of faith
teach.note: Quick consolidation: pupils say the six pillars in a chain, one each. Praise accuracy.

practice: Give two reasons why Allah sent messengers.
Complete: Muhammad ﷺ is the Seal of the Prophets, which means he is the ______ prophet.
Explain in one sentence how belief in the Last Day can affect behaviour.
independent: Write a short paragraph on why belief in the Last Day helps a person be honest.
Create a table of three messengers, what you know about each, and their book if any.
Write what ‘do your best and trust Allah’ looks like in a spelling test.
exit: Why is Muhammad ﷺ called the Seal of the Prophets?
What do Muslims believe about al-Qadr in one sentence?
lessons.homework: Write a thank-you note to Allah (du’a) mentioning one test or worry and how you will use tawakkul.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a word bank and visual flow of the Last Day; stretch: explain how al-Qadr and personal responsibility fit together.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Seerah - the early life of the Prophet ﷺ
lessons.title: Arabia and the birth of the Prophet ﷺ
objectives: Describe what Makkah and Arabia were like before Islam
Retell the story of the Year of the Elephant
State when and where the Prophet ﷺ was born

keywords.def: the house of Allah in Makkah built by Ibrahim and Isma’il
the leading tribe of Makkah, the Prophet’s ﷺ tribe
the biography of the Prophet ﷺ
the period of ignorance before Islam

starter: Who is the last messenger of Allah?
What does ‘seerah’ mean?
Name two prophets who came before Muhammad ﷺ.

teach.heading: Arabia before Islam
bullets: Makkah was a trading town in a desert land
The Ka’bah was filled with idols
Tribes fought and the poor were treated badly
Some people still followed the religion of Ibrahim
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and salawat on the Prophet ﷺ. Show a map. Explain that Ibrahim and Isma’il had built the Ka’bah for the worship of Allah alone and that people had drifted into idol worship. Ask: what problems do we face when people forget Allah? Do not include invented details; keep to widely accepted facts.

teach.heading: The Year of the Elephant
bullets: Abrahah, a ruler from Yemen, marched on Makkah with an army and elephants
He wanted to destroy the Ka’bah
Allah sent flocks of birds with stones
Surah al-Fil (105) tells this story
teach.note: Recite or read Surah al-Fil (105) and explain: Abrahah’s army was destroyed. The Quraysh remembered it as the Year of the Elephant. Scholars record that the Prophet ﷺ was born around that year. Ask: what lesson does it teach about the House of Allah and about power?

teach.heading: The birth of the Prophet ﷺ
bullets: Born in Makkah, in the tribe of Quraysh, around 570 CE
His father Abdullah died before he was born
His mother was Aminah, his grandfather Abdul Muttalib
He was named Muhammad, ‘the praised one’
teach.note: Dates: the day of the week (Monday) is authentically reported in Muslim; the precise date is debated, so say ‘around 570 CE’. Do not claim a celebration date as a fact. Ask pupils to place Makkah on the map and draw a mini family tree.

teach.heading: A family tree
bullets: Descended from Prophet Ibrahim through Isma’il
Abdullah, Aminah, Abdul Muttalib, Abu Talib
Born into an honoured but not wealthy home
teach.note: Check understanding: who are the people in the tree and how are they related? Misconception: the Prophet ﷺ was not from a rich background; his uncle Abu Talib later took care of him.

practice: Place these events in order: Year of the Elephant, birth of the Prophet ﷺ, building of the Ka’bah.
What was Abrahah trying to do and what happened?
Name the Prophet’s ﷺ mother and grandfather.
independent: Write a short newspaper report about the Year of the Elephant.
Draw a simple map of Arabia with Makkah marked and two facts about it.
Create a family tree for the Prophet ﷺ with the names learned.
exit: In which tribe was the Prophet ﷺ born?
Which surah tells the story of the elephant?
lessons.homework: Learn Surah al-Fil with its meaning and write three sentences about the lesson.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing cards with captions and pictures of places; stretch: compare the state of Makkah before and after Islam.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Seerah - the early life of the Prophet ﷺ
lessons.title: An orphan with a caring family
objectives: Explain how the Prophet ﷺ grew up without his parents
Describe his time with Halimah and Abdul Muttalib
Identify what we learn about caring for orphans

keywords.def: a child who has lost one or both parents
the woman of Banu Sa’d who nursed the Prophet ﷺ
the Prophet’s ﷺ uncle who protected him for many years
Arabic word for an orphan

starter: In which year was the Prophet ﷺ born, roughly?
Name his mother and father.
Which surah tells of the elephant?

teach.heading: With Halimah in the desert
bullets: Babies were often sent to the desert to grow strong
Halimah from Banu Sa’d nursed the Prophet ﷺ
He returned to his mother Aminah when he was young
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and salawat. This was an Arab custom for healthy air and pure Arabic. Ask: why would the Prophet ﷺ have loved and respected Halimah? (Later reports describe his respect for her; keep wording general.)

teach.heading: Losing his mother
bullets: Aminah died when he was about six years old
Umm Ayman looked after him
His grandfather Abdul Muttalib took him in
teach.note: Be sensitive: some pupils may have experienced loss. Emphasise that Allah looked after His Messenger ﷺ. Qur’an 93:6 asks: ‘Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?’ Use that in English.

teach.heading: Abu Talib’s care
bullets: Abdul Muttalib died when the Prophet ﷺ was about eight
His uncle Abu Talib looked after him
Abu Talib protected him even later in Makkah
Abu Talib did not accept Islam, but he defended his nephew
teach.note: Be factual and respectful: the Prophet ﷺ loved his uncle; Abu Talib remained on his people’s religion until he died. Do not discuss further with Year 6; if asked, say that guidance is in Allah’s hands (Qur’an 28:56).

teach.heading: What we learn about orphans
bullets: Be kind to orphans and support them
Orphans are cared for in Islam
“I and the person who looks after an orphan will be like this in Paradise,” and he held two fingers together
teach.note: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari (Sahl ibn Sa’d): the Prophet ﷺ said ‘I and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this’ and he showed his index and middle fingers. Discuss ways children can help: charity, sponsoring, kind words to classmates who feel alone.

practice: Put in order: Halimah, Aminah dies, Abdul Muttalib, Abu Talib.
Who cared for the Prophet ﷺ after his grandfather died?
Give two ways a Muslim can help an orphan.
independent: Write a diary entry as the young Muhammad ﷺ after moving to his uncle’s home.
Create a flow chart of who cared for him from birth to age twelve.
Plan a class charity idea for orphans and explain how it follows the sunnah.
exit: Who looked after the Prophet ﷺ after Abdul Muttalib?
What did the Prophet ﷺ say about caring for an orphan?
lessons.homework: Ask a family member how your family can support orphans and write a plan.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: sequencing cards with pictures; stretch: explain why caring for orphans is so highly rated in Islam.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Seerah - the early life of the Prophet ﷺ
lessons.title: Al-Amin: the trustworthy and Khadijah
objectives: Explain why the Prophet ﷺ was called al-Amin
Retell the story of the Black Stone
Describe his marriage to Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her)

keywords.def: the trustworthy
the truthful
the Prophet’s ﷺ first wife and the first to believe
a trust that must be returned or protected

starter: Who looked after the Prophet ﷺ after Abdul Muttalib?
What is an orphan?
What does the word ‘amanah’ mean?

teach.heading: Known for honesty
bullets: The Quraysh called him al-Amin and as-Sadiq
People left their valuables with him
He worked as a shepherd and a trader
Honesty was his habit even before prophethood
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: what would make you trust a person with something precious? The Prophet ﷺ was trusted by those who later opposed him; many still kept their trusts with him. This detail is well known in the seerah; keep the wording general.

teach.heading: The story of the Black Stone
bullets: The Ka’bah was rebuilt and the Black Stone needed placing
Tribes argued about who would have the honour
They agreed to accept the next person to enter
Muhammad ﷺ placed it on a cloak so every tribe could lift it
teach.note: Tell it as a story from the seerah (Ibn Ishaq and others). Ask: how did he solve the problem peacefully? Link to akhlaq: wisdom, fairness, sharing credit.

teach.heading: Marriage to Khadijah
bullets: Khadijah was a respected businesswoman of Makkah
She asked him to trade for her; he was honest and successful
They married when he was about twenty-five
She supported him in all that followed
teach.note: Mention that she was known for her good character. Ask: what qualities does a good partner or friend show? Keep to widely accepted facts and avoid specific unverified details of conversations.

teach.heading: A character we copy
bullets: “Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example” (33:21)
Be honest even when no one is watching
Return what you borrow
Help settle arguments fairly
teach.note: Set a challenge for the week: one honest action each day. Ask pupils to say what will be hardest. Link to Surah al-Ahzab 33:21 in English.

practice: What does al-Amin mean and why was he given the title?
Retell the Black Stone story in three sentences.
Name two qualities of Khadijah.
independent: Write a news report about the Prophet ﷺ solving the Black Stone dispute.
Make a ‘trust’ poster listing five ways to be trustworthy at school.
Write a short letter from Khadijah describing why she respected Muhammad ﷺ.
exit: What does al-Amin mean?
How did the Prophet ﷺ solve the problem of the Black Stone?
lessons.homework: Try one honest action each day and write what you did and how you felt.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: captioned sequencing template for the Black Stone story (words and places, no drawn people); stretch: link al-Amin to the Prophet’s later role as messenger.

lessons.title: Taharah: how to make wudu
objectives: Explain why wudu is needed for salah
Perform and describe the steps of wudu in order
Name things that break wudu

keywords.def: the washing of certain body parts before prayer
purity and cleanliness
impurity such as urine or filth
intention

starter: Why did the Quraysh call Muhammad ﷺ al-Amin?
What is an amanah?
Say bismillah and explain why we start with it.

teach.heading: Why wudu?
bullets: “O you who believe, when you rise for prayer, wash your faces and your hands to the elbows ... and your feet to the ankles” (5:6)
Wudu is needed before salah
Cleanliness is part of faith
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Read 5:6 in English and note the parts named. The hadith ‘Purification is half of faith’ is in Sahih Muslim (Abu Malik al-Ash’ari); you can quote it as ‘cleanliness is half of faith’, paraphrased. Ask: how do we feel after washing? Link to being ready to stand before Allah.

teach.heading: The steps of wudu
bullets: Intend in the heart and say bismillah
Wash hands three times
Rinse mouth and nose three times
Wash face three times, then arms to elbows
Wipe head and ears, then wash feet to ankles
teach.note: Demonstrate on camera with water if possible or mime clearly. Pupils copy on mute. Common mistakes: forgetting heels, skipping elbows, wasting water. Mention that the Prophet ﷺ taught us not to waste water even when making wudu (general principle; do not quote exact wording).

teach.heading: What breaks wudu?
bullets: Going to the toilet
Passing wind
Deep sleep
Loss of consciousness
teach.note: Keep it factual and age-appropriate. Explain that if wudu is broken we repeat it before praying. Some details differ between the schools of fiqh; at Year 6 level teach the agreed basics above and tell pupils to ask their parents or teacher for their family’s school (madhhab) on other matters.

teach.heading: Du’a after wudu and etiquette
bullets: Say the shahadah after wudu
Use only the water you need
Dry your hands and be tidy
Make wudu with calm, not rushing
teach.note: Teach the shahadah after wudu: ‘Ashhadu an la ilaha illallah wahdahu la sharika lah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan abduhu wa rasuluh.’ This is reported in Sahih Muslim (Umar). Practise slowly together.

practice: Put the steps of wudu in the correct order (cards).
List three things that break wudu.
Why should we avoid wasting water during wudu?
independent: Make a step-by-step wudu guide for a younger child with drawings.
Write a paragraph on the meaning of taharah.
Role-play: explain wudu to a new Muslim friend.
exit: Name the first three steps of wudu.
Name two things that break wudu.
lessons.homework: Make wudu at home with a family member watching, and ask them to check each step.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: picture sequence; stretch: explain the wisdom behind washing the particular parts in wudu.

lessons.title: Salah: the daily meeting with Allah
objectives: Name the five daily prayers and their rak’ahs
Explain why salah is important
Describe the main actions in one rak’ah

keywords.def: the ritual prayer, the second pillar of Islam
one unit of prayer
the direction of the Ka’bah
prostration with the forehead on the ground

starter: Name the first step of wudu.
What do we say after finishing wudu?
Which pillar of Islam is salah?

teach.heading: Why do we pray?
bullets: “Establish prayer for My remembrance” (20:14)
Salah connects us to Allah five times a day
It teaches discipline, humility and gratitude
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: who do you talk to when you are worried or happy? Salah is our appointment with Allah. Say that the five daily prayers were made obligatory on the night of the Mi’raj (we will study this in Year 8).

teach.heading: The five prayers
bullets: Fajr: 2 rak’ahs before sunrise
Dhuhr: 4 rak’ahs after midday
Asr: 4 rak’ahs in the afternoon
Maghrib: 3 rak’ahs after sunset
Isha: 4 rak’ahs at night
teach.note: Show a prayer timetable for the local area. Check in on the obligatory rak’ahs only. Pupils make a mnemonic. Ask: which prayer do you find hardest to keep? Encourage honesty and support.

teach.heading: Inside a rak’ah
bullets: Stand facing the qiblah, say Allahu akbar
Recite al-Fatihah and a short surah
Bow (ruku’), stand, then prostrate (sujud)
Sit between two sujuds and repeat
teach.note: Demonstrate carefully. At the end of the second rak’ah (and last) we sit for tashahhud then give salam to right and left. Remind pupils that adults will correct details; we are learning the outline. Mention the beauty of sujud: ‘the closest a servant is to his Lord is while in prostration’ (Sahih Muslim, Abu Hurayrah) - paraphrase is fine.

teach.heading: Praying with khushu’
bullets: Put away distractions and slow down
Understand what you recite
Pray on time
Ask Allah in sujud
teach.note: Ask pupils to share one tip for staying focused. Link to ihsan from lesson 4: worship as if you see Him.

practice: Complete the table of five prayers and rak’ahs.
Put the actions of a rak’ah in order.
Give two benefits of praying on time.
independent: Make a prayer chart for a week to track the five prayers.
Write a paragraph: ‘Why salah matters to a Muslim’.
Create a poster showing the positions of prayer with the du’a said in each.
exit: How many rak’ahs are in Maghrib?
What do we recite in every rak’ah?
lessons.homework: Use your prayer chart and write down which prayers you managed on time and why.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: position cards; stretch: explain the meaning of al-Fatihah verse by verse.

lessons.title: Akhlaq: truthfulness, kindness and good words
objectives: Recall and explain three hadith about good character
Apply them to school and home scenarios
Review the half-term’s learning

keywords.def: character and manners
charity: any good deed given for Allah’s sake
a report of the words or actions of the Prophet ﷺ
truthfulness

starter: Name the five prayers.
State two things that break wudu.
Recall one fact about Khadijah.

teach.heading: The best of character
bullets: The Prophet ﷺ was sent to perfect good character
“Indeed you are of a great character” (68:4)
Good manners are worship
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Qur’an 68:4 is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. Ask: what does ‘character’ mean? Brainstorm good behaviours at school and home.

teach.heading: Smiling is charity
bullets: “Your smiling in the face of your brother is charity” (Tirmidhi)
Small acts count as sadaqah
Greet people with salam
Be cheerful and kind
teach.note: This hadith is recorded by at-Tirmidhi and is graded hasan/sahih; you can use it safely with the attribution. Ask pupils for other small charity acts (clearing the table, helping with bags). Challenge: smile at someone who looks sad today.

teach.heading: Love for others what you love for yourself
bullets: “None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself”
Narrated by Anas in Bukhari and Muslim
Share, include others, avoid jealousy
teach.note: Ask: what do you love for yourself? (fair play, kindness, friends). Then: would you want others to have it too? Role-play a scene at playtime: a child is left out.

teach.heading: Say good or stay silent
bullets: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say good or keep silent”
Bukhari and Muslim
No lying, mocking or gossip
Think before you speak
teach.note: Talk about online speech too: messages and group chats count. Use the THINK idea (is it true, helpful, kind?), as a school rule not a hadith. Ask pupils to give a rewording of a harsh sentence into a kind one.

teach.heading: Review and reflection
bullets: Tawhid and the six pillars
Early life of the Prophet ﷺ
Wudu and salah
What will you improve this month?
teach.note: Use the final slide for a quick quiz and for each pupil to choose a personal akhlaq goal. Close with du’a: ‘O Allah, as You made my creation good, make my character good.’ (This du’a is reported by Imam Ahmad and graded sahih by many scholars.)

practice: Match each hadith to its message (smile, love for brother, good speech).
Rewrite a rude sentence into a kind one.
Give two examples of charity that cost no money.
independent: Write a short story where a child follows one of the hadith.
Create an ‘akhlaq action plan’ with three goals and how you will check them.
Make five quiz questions on this half-term’s lessons with answers.
exit: Say one hadith about character in your own words.
What akhlaq goal will you work on and how?
lessons.homework: Carry out your akhlaq goal for five days and keep a short log.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: scenario cards with pictures; stretch: link each hadith to a verse or lesson from earlier in the unit.
